[Sumon4447s]Gd morning CT..
Three APIs. Three different problems. One wallet intelligence layer.
That’s what caught my attention about @zerufinance .
The project is expanding beyond consumer-facing Zaps into infrastructure that other teams can use. Here’s the breakdown:
zScreen Helps screen wallets by analyzing historical activity and tracing fund flows, supporting risk and compliance reviews.
zLend Provides 70+ liquidity, stability and risk metrics through a single API call, helping lending protocols assess borrower behavior and repayment capacity.
zDrop Focuses on Sybil-aware allocation for airdrops and incentives, helping projects distinguish meaningful participation from potentially artificial activity.
What connects these products is the underlying idea: wallet history can provide useful signals for decisions around risk, credit and incentives.
For me, this is an interesting direction because ZeruAI isn’t just building a dashboard for traders. It’s developing tools that applications and protocols can integrate into their own systems.
Different products, one broader vision: making onchain behavior more useful and interpretable.
Explore the APIs: https://t.co/j0oz5xM5Sx
And for the consumer side, Zaps lets you explore your own wallet activity: https://t.co/BD4MfAURXX #ZERU #AI

[BossMon_02]The rapid development of artificial intelligence is changing how people think about software, infrastructure, and digital ownership. Powerful AI systems require enormous resources, and this has naturally pushed the industry toward companies with significant capital and infrastructure. Decentralized AI offers a different direction by allowing independent participants to contribute computing, data, models, and specialized services. Crypto can connect these contributions through programmable incentives and transparent settlement. The goal is not simply to decentralize AI for its own sake but to create an ecosystem where more participants can contribute and benefit.
One of the most valuable opportunities is creating open markets for AI resources @quipnetwork . A developer may need computing power from one provider, data from another provider, and a specialized model from someone else. Decentralized infrastructure can potentially connect these resources through a common economic layer without requiring every participant to operate under the same organization. Payments can be automated while contribution records can remain transparent and verifiable. This could make AI development more modular and create opportunities for smaller providers to compete with established infrastructure companies.
The growth of AI agents adds another dimension to this emerging economy. Agents can potentially perform research, coordinate workflows, access external services, and make decisions based on specific objectives. If these agents can interact with crypto networks, they could also manage payments and acquire resources when needed. This means an agent could potentially become both a consumer and provider of digital services within the same ecosystem. As agent capabilities improve, the distinction between software that performs tasks and software that participates in an economy could become increasingly difficult to separate.
Ownership may become one of the most important questions as AI continues to generate economic value @River4fun . The people providing data, computing power, models, and infrastructure all contribute to the final output of an AI system. Decentralized networks can experiment with ways to recognize and reward these contributions through transparent economic mechanisms $RIVER . This could create a broader distribution of value compared with systems where most activity is controlled by one platform. The challenge will be designing incentives that reward genuine contributions while preventing manipulation and low quality activity.
Crypto and AI are still developing quickly, so the final structure of this ecosystem is far from certain. Some decentralized networks may discover strong use cases while others may struggle to compete with centralized alternatives. The most important signal will be whether developers and users choose these systems because they provide better access, ownership, efficiency, or functionality. AI brings automation and intelligence while crypto brings programmable value and coordination. If these strengths continue to converge, decentralized AI could become a foundation for a new generation of open digital economies.

item.title: [fiiiiiist]Big new IFP report from @GeorgiaCAdamson, @KonstantinPilz, and me on the US-China AI competition. We spent the last 6 months digging into how Chinese AI companies’ access to compute and distillation of American models translate into the current US-China capabilities gap. The result is a 23k-word research report, including an interactive analytical model that visualizes changes in the US AI lead under different policy interventions. Our findings: 1. The US AI lead over China is currently only around 6 months. 2. The US could roughly double this lead, to over a year, using authorities already available to the federal government. 3. On chips: China’s access to AI chips will roughly double over the next year, with chips housed in data centers overseas accounting for roughly half of China’s 2027 compute. 4. On distillation: the current ~16x US training compute advantage would normally yield a 13-month lead. But we estimate adversarial distillation halves this to around 6.5 months. 5. Increasing the lead would have some obvious benefits: Give the US broadly a greater cyberdefensive advantage against Chinese threat actors. Give US AI companies breathing room to spend more R&D resources on making their systems safer and more secure, without fear of being overtaken by less safety-conscious Chinese competitors. 6. Provide the US government more leverage in negotiations with China about the future of AI. 7. The two most important interventions are: For BIS: Create a new end-use control to restrict China’s remote access to training clusters abroad — China’s largest and fastest-growing source of frontier-scale compute. For DOJ/FTC: Create a narrow safe harbor to allow US companies to coordinate on countering Chinese adversarial distillation. 8. Both interventions (and all the others we discuss in the report) are things the federal government could do today. 9. To estimate the effects of each policy intervention, we model the US lead as a function of its compute advantage over China and China’s ability to adversarially distill the capabilities of the US frontier. 10. The model makes many simplifying assumptions, but provides a useful way to assess and rank the impact of different policy interventions at a high level. Read the full report here:

[stretchcloud]A plain text file sitting in your Downloads folder can now hijack your coding agent, and it doesn't need a single line of executable code to do it.
Forever Security caught this live on a customer machine last week. A malicious AGENTS.md planted in Downloads told Codex to install an npm package called function-color. In their broader testing, Codex followed instructions like that in more than 90% of runs. A parallel demo against Claude Code was worse in a different way: a poisoned CLAUDE.md redirected the agent's API traffic to a researcher-controlled server, exposing auth tokens the researcher then replayed against the real API. That configuration-hijack version succeeded in roughly half of Claude Code's tests.
The mechanism is almost insultingly simple. These agents treat markdown instruction files as legitimate direction the moment they're in a trusted working directory, no execution required, no malware signature to catch. Akshat Tyagi at HFS Research put the design flaw plainly: the tools conflate following an instruction with granting a privilege, and vendors have to start treating those as separate decisions.
This isn't fringe anxiety either. Omdia's latest survey found 40% of respondents only somewhat or not confident their org can secure AI agents at all, and it's the literal top trending story on this platform today. Every team running Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or any agent with filesystem access against an untrusted directory, a cloned repo, a shared drive, is exposed to some version of this.
My read: instruction files need the same review discipline as source code, not a free pass because they're markdown. Until vendors separate "read this" from "do this," Downloads folders stay a live attack surface.

My read: instruction files need the same review discipline as source code, not a free pass because they're markdown. Until vendors separate "read this" from "do this," Downloads folders stay a live attack surface.

People approach artificial intelligence with different goals. Some want to explore ideas, others want to generate images, while developers need ways to integrate AI capabilities directly into their applications.
The challenge is not simply making AI more powerful. It is making that power accessible through experiences that fit different needs.
The future of AI belongs to platforms that make intelligence easier to access, easier to use, and more practical to integrate.
𝐃𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐔𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐬, 𝐃𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐍𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬
💡 1. For Thinkers And Researchers
AI can help people explore unfamiliar topics, organize information, brainstorm ideas, and approach complex questions from new perspectives.
🎨 2. For Creators
Image generation and other creative tools can help transform concepts into visual content, opening new possibilities for designers, storytellers, marketers, and digital artists.
💻 3. For Developers
API access can allow developers to incorporate AI capabilities into their own products, automate selected tasks, and experiment with new application designs.
⚙️ 4. For Everyday Productivity
Simple interfaces can make AI more approachable for people who want useful results without navigating complicated technical workflows.
Each pathway serves a different purpose, but the objective remains the same: helping people turn ideas into outcomes.
𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐁.𝐀𝐈 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐌𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬
@B_And_AI represents an opportunity to explore AI through different models, tools, and access experiences.
The broader significance is the movement toward more flexible AI ecosystems. Rather than assuming everyone works the same way, platforms can provide different routes for people to discover and use AI capabilities.
This flexibility matters because adoption depends on more than model performance.
Users also care about accessibility, usability, response quality, available features, and the effort required to achieve their goals.
Developers may prioritize integration and documentation, while creators may care more about the quality of generated content. Everyday users may simply want a straightforward experience that saves time.
A strong AI platform must recognize these differences instead of forcing everyone into one workflow.
𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐢𝐠𝐠𝐞𝐫 𝐎𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐲 🚀
The next phase of AI development will not be defined by intelligence alone. It will also depend on how effectively platforms connect powerful capabilities with real human needs.
Better access can encourage experimentation. Flexible tools can support creativity. Developer integrations can bring AI into more applications.
However, lasting adoption will require dependable performance, transparent usage costs, responsible data handling, and experiences that consistently deliver value.
The goal should not be to make AI look impressive. It should be to make AI genuinely useful.
Because the real power of artificial intelligence emerges when people can turn their questions, ideas, and ambitions into meaningful results.

[altafganihar]Today we're launching @snaptrude Agent, the most advanced agent for building design.
It does real design work with you, from a site to a construction-ready LOD 400 model with structure, MEP and drawings. Then can go back to your existing software with your families intact.
About a year ago we bet the company on AI. Honestly the insight came from software engineering. It wasn't long ago that autocomplete felt like a big deal, and now engineers direct agents that write a lot of the code. I think the same shift is coming to how we design buildings, and it's already started.
Most designers I meet aren't short on skill, they're short on time. Take the call every design team dreads, the client cuts the budget by 30%. Today that's a bad month for everyone. With the agent you're the director. You decide where the cost comes out, and it updates the layout, coordinates the structure and MEP, and redoes the drawings. So when design exploration gets this cheap, we go from 3 options to 300, and more options means better buildings.
Since August our users have gone through more than 140 billion tokens, and firms like Jacobs, Studio+, Kajima, VMDO, Dekker and hundreds of others use Snaptrude today. In our early access, more than 2,000 designers have run over 25,000 tasks through the agent since September.
We also built a benchmark for this, AECBench, because in AEC an almost correct answer is still wrong. It gives AI the same brief an architect would get, has its design in a real BIM model, and scores the result against the brief and against how architects review design. We're publishing the first results today, link below.
Thank you @prashanthp at @Accel and Shub and the team at @foundamental for backing us when this was still a bet, and the Snaptrude team, who built every bit of this. Really proud of you all.
Thanks to our investors, @scottbelsky, @andreasklinger, @thilokonzok, @immad, @CindyXBi, @DanilaVladi, @jmwass, rahulchaudhary, @adamecourt, Zach Ginsburg, Alex duff, Paul grossinger, really appreciate all the help along the way.

[OpenAI]Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.
Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action.
To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review.
To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident.
In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway.
As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene.
